situational4.title: Situational writing · 6 Primary 4 tasks with models

bands.label: 6 · All three points covered, each with a supporting detail
5 · All three covered, one of them thin
4 · Correct format and greeting, tone right, very few errors

tasks.task:
Your classmate Hui Ling was absent yesterday. Write her a short note.

You should include:
• what she missed in class
• the homework that was given
• an offer to help

Write about 60 to 80 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to tell her what happened. Audience: a classmate — informal. Context: three points, each needing one detail.
tasks.model:
Hi Hui Ling,

I hope you are feeling better. You missed quite a lot yesterday.

In Science we started the new topic on magnets, and Mr Lee did an experiment with iron filings on a sheet of paper. It was the best lesson we have had this term.

For homework we have to finish Workbook pages 24 to 26, and write five sentences about what we saw in the experiment. It is due on Friday.

If you like, I can come over on Wednesday after school and show you my notes, because the experiment is hard to explain in writing.

Get well soon!

Your friend,
Dinesh
tasks.why: All three points are covered and each one carries a detail: not just 'we did Science' but which topic and which experiment; not just 'there is homework' but the pages and the due date; not just 'I can help' but when, and why helping in person would be better. The tone is friendly throughout and the note opens and closes properly.

tasks.task:
Your aunt sent you a birthday present. Write her an email.

You should include:
• thanks for the present
• what you have done with it so far
• news about something happening at school

Write about 60 to 80 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to thank and to share news. Audience: an aunt you know well — warm and informal. Context: three points.
tasks.model:
To: aunty_meena@email.com
Subject: Thank you for the paint set!

Dear Aunty Meena,

Thank you so much for the watercolour set you sent for my birthday. It arrived on Saturday morning, and I was very surprised because I had not told anybody that I wanted one.

I have already used it twice. On Sunday I painted the tree outside our kitchen window, and yesterday I painted our neighbour's cat, which came out looking more like a rabbit. My mother has put both of them on the fridge anyway.

At school we are getting ready for Racial Harmony Day next month. My class is doing a dance, and I have been chosen to be in the second row, which I am quite pleased about.

Thank you again. I will send you a photograph of my next painting, if it goes better than the cat did.

Love,
Sarah
tasks.why: The thanks are specific rather than general, and the second point does the most work: two real paintings, one of which went wrong, which is far more interesting than 'I have used it a lot'. The school news is a genuine piece of news with a detail attached. The closing line ties back to the joke, which is a nice touch at this level but not required.

tasks.task:
You borrowed your cousin's book and spilt a drink on it. Write him a message.

You should include:
• what happened
• an apology
• what you will do about it

Write about 60 to 80 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to apologise. Audience: a cousin — informal, but the tone must be genuinely sorry, not jokey.
tasks.model:
Hi Marcus,

I have some bad news about your book. I was reading it at the kitchen table yesterday evening and I knocked over a glass of Milo. The first twenty pages are stained brown and two of them are stuck together at the corner.

I am really sorry. It was completely my fault — I should not have been drinking anything next to it.

I have looked the book up online and it costs $14.90. I have $9 saved and I will have the rest by the end of the month, so I would like to buy you a new copy. If you would rather have it sooner, I can ask my mother and pay her back.

Sorry again. I will not borrow anything of yours near a drink again.

Dinesh
tasks.why: The apology works because the damage is described honestly and in detail before the sorry, rather than after it. Blame is accepted without excuses. The third point is concrete — a price, an amount saved, a date, and an alternative — which is what turns an apology into a solution.

tasks.task:
Your school is holding a Sports Day. Write an email inviting your grandfather.

You should include:
• when and where it is
• what you will be taking part in
• how he can get there

Write about 60 to 80 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to invite. Audience: your grandfather — warm and clear. Context: he needs practical information, so the third point matters as much as the first two.
tasks.model:
To: ah_gong@email.com
Subject: Come to my Sports Day!

Dear Ah Gong,

Our school Sports Day is on Saturday 12 July, from 8 a.m. to 12 noon, on the school field.

I am running in the 100 metres at about 9.15, and I am in the class relay, which is the last event.

You can take bus 156 from your block and get off at the fourth stop, right outside our gate. If you would rather not, my father can fetch you at half past seven.

Please come!

Love,
Sarah
tasks.why: Every one of the three points carries a real detail, and the third — bus number, which stop, how long, plus an alternative — is the one most pupils leave thin. The joke about Amirul keeps the tone warm without losing the information. Notice that the writer tells him where she will be looking for him, which shows she has thought about the reader.

tasks.task:
You are the class monitor. The classroom cupboard is untidy. Write a notice for the class noticeboard.

You should include:
• what the problem is
• what everybody should do
• when it must be done by

Write about 60 to 80 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to tell everybody what to do. Audience: your classmates — plain and polite, not bossy. Context: a notice, so no greeting and no sign-off, but put your name at the end.
tasks.model:
PLEASE HELP: OUR CLASS CUPBOARD

THE PROBLEM
The cupboard at the back of the classroom is so full that the door no longer shuts properly. Two files fell out on Monday and the pages got mixed up. There are also three lunchboxes in there that have been left for more than a week.

WHAT TO DO
Please take out anything of yours that does not belong in school and bring it home. Put files on the top shelf, art materials on the middle shelf, and PE things on the bottom shelf. If something is not yours, leave it on my desk and I will try to find the owner.

BY WHEN
Please do this before recess on Friday. Mrs Ong will be checking the cupboard that afternoon.

Thank you!
Sarah (class monitor)
tasks.why: A notice has no 'Dear' and no 'Yours sincerely', and this one does not pretend to be a letter. The three headings let a classmate find what they need without reading it all. The instructions are specific enough to follow — which shelf for what — and the deadline has a reason attached, which makes it far more likely to be obeyed than a bare date.

tasks.task:
You went on a school excursion last week. Write to your friend who has moved away.

You should include:
• where you went
• the best part of the day
• one thing that went wrong

Write about 60 to 80 words.
tasks.pac: Purpose: to describe. Audience: a friend — informal and chatty. Context: three points; the third is the one that makes the email worth reading.
tasks.model:
To: jia_wei@email.com
Subject: Our trip to the wetland reserve

Hi Jia Wei,

You missed a good one. Last Thursday our level went to the wetland reserve at Sungei Buloh.

The best part was the mudskippers. One hopped onto a root a metre from the boardwalk and sat staring at us.

The thing that went wrong was our worksheet. Faizal put it on the railing for one second and the wind took it into the water, so we redid it from memory on the bus.

How is your new school?

Your friend,
Dinesh
tasks.why: The three points are all covered with detail, and the writer knows that the disaster is the most entertaining part, so it gets the fullest paragraph. Small precise facts — eleven minutes of rain, eight centimetres, station three — do more than adjectives. The two questions at the end keep it a real conversation rather than a report.

situational4.instruction: Write about 60 to 80 words. Cover all three points, each with one supporting detail. Marks: 6 for task fulfilment, 4 for language and format.

oral3.title: Walking or riding to school
oral3.stimulus:
SCHOOL NEWSLETTER · HOW WE GET HERE
How our pupils travel to school
Of the pupils who live within one kilometre of the school, 56% still come by car. The most common reason parents gave was the morning rush, not distance or weather.

questions.q: Looking at this chart, what stands out to you?
questions.model: The chart shows that the car is by far the most common way pupils get to school, at 41%, while only about one in five walks. What I find most surprising is the line underneath. More than half of the pupils who live within one kilometre still come by car, and a kilometre is a walk of about twelve minutes. So the problem is not really distance. The newsletter says the main reason parents gave was the morning rush, which suggests that families are short of time rather than short of options.

questions.q: How do you get to school, and what do you like or dislike about it?
questions.model: I walk, because I live in the block behind the school, and it takes me about eight minutes. What I like best is that I walk with my neighbour Siti and we talk the whole way, which means I arrive awake instead of half asleep. What I dislike is the rain. Twice last term I arrived with wet socks and had to sit in them all morning, and on those days I did wish we had a car.

questions.q: What could a school do to encourage more pupils to walk?
questions.model: I think a school should make walking feel organised rather than just allowed. One idea I have read about is a walking bus, where a parent walks a fixed route at a fixed time and children join along the way. That would help with the morning rush, because parents would not each have to make their own trip. Secondly, I would put up a covered walkway on the busiest path, since rain is the reason most people give up walking. Finally, I would give each class a chart of how many walking days it has managed in a month, because my class will compete over absolutely anything.

oral3.title: Looking after a pet
oral3.stimulus:
PET SHOP NOTICE · BEFORE YOU BUY
Is your family ready for a pet?
A rabbit lives for 8 to 12 years. It needs fresh hay every day, a clean cage twice a week, and time outside the cage. Many rabbits are given away in their first year, and the most common reason is that nobody had time.

questions.q: What does this notice tell you about keeping a rabbit?
questions.model: It tells me that a rabbit is a lot more work than I would have guessed. It needs fresh hay every single day and time outside its cage every day, and the cage has to be cleaned twice a week. The part that surprised me most is that a rabbit can live for eight to twelve years, which is almost as long as I have been alive. The notice also says many rabbits are given away in the first year because nobody had time, so I think the shop is trying to make families think carefully first.

questions.q: Tell me about an animal you have looked after, or one you would like to look after.
questions.model: My family looks after my neighbour's cat, Tiger, whenever they travel. It is my job to feed him in the morning and change his water. The first time, I put down too much food and my mother said he would be sick, so now I use the small cup that came with the packet. What I like is that he waits by the door at the same time every morning. What I did not expect is how much he sheds. I have to sweep the corridor outside our flat every day he stays with us.

questions.q: What should a family think about before getting a pet?
questions.model: I think the first thing to ask is who will actually do the work, because in my experience the person who wants the pet most is not always the person who ends up feeding it. The second thing is time. This notice says rabbits need something every single day, so a family that is out from morning until night should probably choose a pet that needs less, or none at all. The last thing I would think about is how long the animal lives. If a rabbit lives for ten years, a Primary 3 pupil getting one now will be in secondary school before it is old, and somebody has to plan for that.

oral3.title: Helping at home
oral3.stimulus:
FAMILY LIFE SURVEY · PRIMARY PUPILS
Which jobs do children do at home?
In a survey of 600 primary pupils, 18% said they did no household jobs at all. Pupils who had one regular job they were in charge of were far more likely to keep doing it than pupils who were asked each time.

questions.q: What do you notice about this survey?
questions.model: I notice that the jobs children do most are the ones closest to themselves. More than half tidy their own room, but fewer than one in five hangs the laundry, which is a job for the whole family rather than just for you. I also noticed that 18% said they did nothing at all, which is about one child in every six. The most useful part is the last sentence: children who were in charge of one job kept doing it, and children who were asked each time did not. That suggests the job should be yours rather than something you are told to do.

questions.q: What jobs do you do at home? Tell me about one of them.
questions.model: I am in charge of the rubbish. Every evening after dinner I tie the bag and take it down to the chute on our floor. It is not a difficult job, but I have to remember it without being told, and at the beginning I forgot about three times a week. What helped was that my father stopped reminding me. The first time the kitchen started to smell, I noticed it myself, and I have not forgotten since. I also wash the rice now on Sundays, because my grandmother taught me how many times to rinse it.

questions.q: Do you think children should have to help at home? Why?
questions.model: Yes, I think so, for two reasons. The first is fairness. Everybody in a family uses the plates and makes the mess, so it is not right for one or two people to do all the clearing up. The second reason is that these are things we will all need to do one day anyway, and it is much easier to learn them at nine than to learn them all at once when you are older. I would add one thing, though. I think it works better when a child is given one job to own rather than being asked to help with whatever is left, because this survey says exactly that.

readAloud3.text: Our class has a tortoise called Bruce. He is older than everybody in the room, including Mrs Ong. He moves so slowly that we once thought he had stopped moving altogether, and Faizal nearly cried. Then Bruce turned his head, very slightly, and looked at us as though we had been extremely rude. He eats cabbage on Thursdays, sleeps most of the rest of the week, and has never once done anything exciting. He is the most popular member of our class.
notes: 'Bruce' — one clear syllable. Do not rush past it; the name is part of the joke.
Pause at the commas in the fifth sentence (“He eats cabbage on Thursdays…”). It has three parts.
Final consonants: moves, stopped, turned, looked, eats, sleeps.
Stress 'never once' and 'most popular' — the contrast is the point of the passage.
Slow down for the last sentence and let it land. Do not smile it away.

readAloud3.text: There is a bird in Singapore that can copy almost any sound it hears. The common mynah has been recorded imitating car alarms, mobile phone ringtones and, in one case, the whistle a man used to call his dog. The dog, it is said, came running three times before anybody worked out what was happening. Scientists think mynahs copy sounds to mark out territory. Whatever the reason, it means that some of the noises you hear outside your window in the morning were not made by a machine at all.
notes: 'mynah' — MY-na. Say it clearly the first time; it is the key word.
The list in the second sentence has three items. Pause before 'and, in one case'.
Final consonants: recorded, imitating, worked, mark, machine.
Stress 'three times' — it is the funny detail.
The last sentence is a mild surprise. Slow slightly on 'not made by a machine at all'.

readAloud3.text: My mother keeps a list on the fridge of everything she has ever lent to a neighbour. There are fourteen items on it. Next to eleven of them she has written a date, a name and a small tick. Next to the other three she has written a date and a name and nothing else, and she has been writing nothing else beside those three for about six years. She says she is not annoyed. She says she keeps the list only so that she remembers what she owns. Nobody in our family believes this, and nobody says so.
notes: Numbers carry this passage: 'fourteen', 'eleven', 'three', 'six years'. Say each one clearly.
Pause after 'a date, a name and a small tick' before the next sentence.
Do not rush 'and she has been writing nothing else beside those three for about six years'. Breathe after 'three'.
The two sentences beginning 'She says' should sound flat and innocent. That is where the humour is.
Land firmly on the last sentence, and pause a beat before 'and nobody says so'.
